In late September the priest climbed the terraces to bless the harvest and found the steps empty. Alonso was among the rows, sharing the pickers' sausage and laughing. Rafael, watching him, felt oddly ______. He did not go down to him. He took the bread from his own satchel, broke it in two, and set half on the empty step where Alonso usually sat.

his shirts pinned in a row he straightened twice,
each collar facing the sea.
Elodie, from the next building, waits too,
her sheets heavy, her arms folded,
saying the line is nothing, the shirts are nothing,
he only washes them that way because his mother did.
Thunder moves off toward Toulon.
He shrugs and agrees, the shirts are nothing,
and turns one sleeve so the cuff lies flat.
When the sun breaks, a gull lands on his line,
and Armand, ______, waves it off with his hat
before it can step near a white collar,
then laughs as if he had meant to lose the hat,

items.passage: Ferries make poor classrooms. Savitri, unsure, began reading out the old hour. Xinyi listened, ______, and then stepped forward, took the chalk from the clerk's ledge, and wrote the right hour in a small, plain hand before returning to her place at the edge of the group.

The plan was mine: I had told the headmistress that Kian was my uncle, so the room would be lent for free. On the third afternoon the headmistress came in and asked him how my grandmother was keeping. Kian, ______, answered that she was well and asked after the headmistress's son. items.passage: Diesel and overripe tomatoes thickened the air at the Saturday market off Greenmarket Square, and Aster's table held less than half of what it had the year before. Sipho watched his grandmother arrange the tomatoes in a single row, then a pyramid, then a row again, pressing each with her thumb before setting it down. He had taken this for a way of hiding how few there were. Near noon a woman in a green headscarf stopped and asked whether Aster had any of the small yellow ones from last spring. Aster lifted a cloth from a basket under the table. Inside were six yellow tomatoes, each wrapped in newspaper, each with a penciled name: the regulars who had bought them every week before the drought. She found the woman's name and handed the parcel over without taking money. Sipho looked at the five still in the basket. Aster slid it back under the table and returned to pressing the red ones, one by one, while the crowd moved past.

items.passage: Why did Hedwig wind the clocks backward? Kalani, the landlord's son, had noticed it on three rent days running: while her father counted coins at the bench of the little Havana shop, she moved along the wall of clocks and turned each key the wrong way, gently, until it resisted, and then let it go. He took it for a girl's idle mischief and said nothing, since his own father disliked complaints. On the fourth rent day his father asked to see the shop's account book. Hedwig's father went pale and reached for the drawer, but Hedwig was quicker; she set the book on the counter herself, opened to a page in her own neat hand, and stepped back to the clocks. Kalani, reading over his father's shoulder, saw that every entry was dated a week before the coins had truly come in. His father nodded and closed the book. Hedwig turned one more key the wrong way and looked at Kalani, and he held her gaze without a word.

items.passage: "Father, the postmaster says the river road is shorter," I told him, spreading the map across the counter. Taeyang did not look at it. __He had folded the corner of every map he owned toward the north, a habit I took for the neatness of a clerk.__ Outside, a cart of melons rolled past the little post office, and the clerk inside weighed our parcel twice, frowning at the scale as though it had insulted him. I paid the fee from my own purse, counting the coins in English under my breath, which made the clerk smile. We had come to send a parcel to my aunt, though Father had written nothing on the label but a name. When the clerk asked where it should go, Father answered with the name of a village I had never once heard him say aloud. He took the map from me, opened its folded corner, and pressed his thumbnail against a small dot beside a river that does not run anywhere near Shanghai. Then he handed the map back to me and asked whether the river road was paved.

items.passage: Three rules governed the chess club on the promenade, and Radek had written them himself on a card above the door: no talking during play, no coffee near the boards, no lessons for another member's pupils. __Vesna kept her own clock in a velvet bag, though the club had owned electric ones for twenty years.__ That afternoon the wind off the water rattled the windows, and two old men argued about whether the gulls were louder this year. Radek's pupil, a boy of eleven, sat across from him practicing the sealed move, the old custom of writing a move in an envelope when a game is paused overnight. Hardly anyone under sixty in the club still knew how to do it properly. The boy kept forgetting to stop the clock before he wrote. At six, Vesna rose, crossed to Radek's table, and set the velvet bag beside the envelope. She left without a word. Inside was her clock, its two buttons worn pale, with a slip of paper wedged under the stop lever.

items.passage: Buckets of silt came up the cellar steps all morning, and by noon my brother and I had saved a tin box of our mother's letters. __Talon, who had studied her language for two years in Flagstaff, offered to read them aloud while I laid the pages on the porch to dry.__ Wind moved across the plateau, and a neighbor's dog kept stealing the clothespins I had set out for the wet blankets. I chased it twice and gave up. Talon read slowly, sometimes stopping to rub a smeared word with his thumb. In one letter, he said, she called our father a patient man. Near dusk I found a second copy of that letter folded inside an envelope, written in her careful English for a cousin who could not read Diné. Where Talon had said patient, she had written stubborn as a fence post. I read it twice. When Talon came out with coffee, I handed him the envelope, and he set his cup down on the step without drinking. "Chayton," he said, and then said nothing else.

items.passage: Promises are cheap on a tram line. That was my mother's saying, and I repeated it the winter I rode Moana's bus each morning to the weaving cooperative on Ponsonby Road. __Moana kept a child's drawing of a red kite pinned above the fare box, its corners curling from the heat of the engine.__ At the cooperative we were finishing a flax mat for a wedding, and I spent most days arguing with the other women about a border pattern none of us would agree to tighten. One morning Moana missed my stop and drove two streets past it before he noticed, apologizing so many times that I laughed at him. In late August his route changed, and a new driver took the bus. The drawing was gone from above the fare box. That Saturday, walking home, I saw Moana on the hill above the harbor, holding the string of a red kite while a small girl in a borrowed coat ran beneath it, shouting at the wind.

items.passage: "We called your grandfather Arslan in those days," Kerem said, for the third time that week, and Emre stabbed at his rice. Kerem ran the camp dining hall as if it were a ship, banging a ladle on the counter at seven sharp and grumbling that boys today could not peel an onion. Emre told the other counselors the old man was a fossil in an apron. He was not lying, exactly; he was leaving things out. My father had sailed for Fujian when I was nine and had sent two letters since. Baoyu never spoke of him. We argued about leaves for six autumns, loudly enough that the neighbors leaned out of their windows. One year he brought a small tin box along with the rake and set it on the fountain's rim; I did not open it, and he did not mention it. The seventh October he did not come. A boy brought the rake and the tin box to the gate with a note in Baoyu's hand: the leaves are yours to decide now.
